UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                      )
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C                            )                 Docket No. ER26-3380-000
                                                      )



                         COMMENTS OF ADVANCED ENERGY UNITED

         Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”)

Rules of Practice and Procedures,1 Advanced Energy United2 (“United”) submits these

comments in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) revisions to the PJM Open

Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and the Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load

Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”).3 United

generally supports PJM’s July 31, 2026, filing as the best available solution to address the

pressing challenge of rapid load growth and slow resource entry in a manner that avoids putting

even greater cost burden on existing customers not contributing to the resource adequacy

shortfall. However, RBP is far from an ideal outcome, and must be implemented in a manner that

avoids perverse and distortionary outcomes that could undermine the investment landscape in

PJM. Advanced Energy United’s comments below point to areas that need clarification and/or

commitment from PJM, both in the context of RBP itself and to improve the region’s resource

adequacy outlook moving forward.



1
  18 C.F.R. § 385.211
2
  Advanced Energy United is a national association of businesses that are making the energy we use secure, clean,
and affordable. Advanced Energy United is the only industry association in the United States that represents the full
range of advanced energy technologies and services, both grid-scale and distributed. Advanced energy includes
energy efficiency, demand response, energy storage, wind, solar, hydro, nuclear, electric vehicles, and more.
3
  PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. “Reliability Backstop Procurement to Address Resource Adequacy Concerns
Stemming from Large Loads” Docket No. ER26-3380-000 (filed July 31, 2026) (“Transmittal Letter”).
                                                                                                                    1
   I.   INTRODUCTION

       PJM is navigating a genuinely difficult situation, and the RBP reflects real effort to

design a workable response under significant time pressure. United and its members have been

active participants throughout the stakeholder process leading to this filing, and the RBP

framework and related Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) proposal as proposed

reflect meaningful refinement from the concepts PJM initially floated through the Critical Issue

Fast Path processes earlier this year and in 2025. For these reasons and because of the urgency of

taking action, United does not oppose the RBP mechanism PJM has proposed.

       United’s support, however, is not without reservation. The comments below identify

specific areas where PJM’s proposal falls short of its own stated objectives, or where PJM’s own

reasoning for excluding otherwise-qualified resources does not withstand scrutiny. United urges

the Commission to direct PJM to act on these issues promptly, for two related reasons. First,

several of the barriers discussed below—particularly with respect to Surplus Interconnection

Service and demand-side resources—unnecessarily constrain the pool of fast-to-deploy capacity

available to the RBP, and addressing them would materially improve PJM’s chances of actually

filling the shortfall the RBP is designed to address. Second, and more broadly, these same

barriers bear directly on the success of PJM’s separate Build Your Own New Capacity

(“BYONC”) initiative and on the durability of investment confidence in PJM generally;

resolving them now will pay dividends well beyond this single procurement. United emphasizes

that RBP was conceived, and must remain, a one-time, bounded response to the specific shortfall

identified in the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction, not a template PJM may invoke unilaterally




                                                                                                   2
 each time a future auction falls short. United’s comments accordingly conclude with specific

recommendations to ensure the mechanism does not outlive its stated purpose.

    II.    COMMENTS

           A. RBP Includes Important Elements that will Contribute to its Success

           PJM should be commended for several elements of the RBP design that will support full

participation by qualified resources and promote fair outcomes for developers navigating the

procurement’s compressed timeline.

           First, United supports the shortfall-charge exception for resources unable to meet their

expected commercial operation date solely due to Network Upgrades, where the resource

demonstrates readiness through test energy and seeks interim deliverability.4 Network Upgrade

costs and schedules represent one of the largest sources of risk facing new capacity development

in PJM today. A meaningful share of the resources best positioned to participate in the RBP are

currently at some stage of the interconnection process, and without this exception, those

resources would bear shortfall-charge risk for delays entirely outside their control, a result that

would needlessly shrink the pool of supply available to the RBP at the exact moment PJM most

needs it to be as large as possible.

           United cautions, however, that this exception addresses only one element of the risk that

projects still in the queue face: it excuses the shortfall charge itself, but developers must still

price uncertain Network Upgrade costs and schedules into their RBP bids, and continue to bear

real cost and schedule risk for as long as their projects remain queued. This exception is a

necessary and well-designed accommodation, but it is not a substitute for PJM continuing to

prioritize a faster, more predictable interconnection process and to resolve Network Upgrade cost


4
    Transmittal Letter at 60.
                                                                                                       3
 and schedule uncertainty that persists even after a generator interconnection agreement is signed.

Both the Commission and PJM should remain actively engaged on these challenges well beyond

the scope of this proceeding.

            Second, United also welcomes PJM’s decision to allow new load to use Surplus

Interconnection Service (“SIS”) capacity to reduce its own RBP obligation as Qualifying RBP

offset UCAP.5 Recognizing SIS-derived capacity as legitimate, usable supply for these purposes

is the right outcome. United notes, however, that this recognition does not currently extend to

allowing SIS-based resources to sell directly into the RBP, an asymmetry United addresses

separately. Nor does it resolve barriers to full utilization of SIS to deliver new capacity to the

PJM region, an issue that United urges PJM to resolve expeditiously outside of the RBP

proceeding, as discussed below.

            Third, United appreciates PJM’s inclusion of Demand Response and DER Aggregation

Resources as eligible sources of Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW, including their use as a

bridge for new load pending availability of generation or storage capacity not yet in service.6

United welcomes this bridge function as one use case among several, but does not read it as

limiting the role Demand Response and DER Aggregation Resources can or should play; these

resources provide durable capacity, energy, and congestion relief value independent of whether

new generation or storage is also under development, and PJM’s Tariff should recognize that

standing value rather than treating demand-side participation as merely transitional. Demand-

side resources are flexible, comparatively affordable, and capable of being deployed quickly

relative to new-build generation, and their inclusion here is a meaningful step, even as United




5
    Id at 36.
6
    Id at 40.
                                                                                                     4
 requests additional flexibility regarding their eligibility to participate as RBP Resources, as

discussed below.

         Fourth, United supports the narrow opt-out PJM has proposed for Electric Distributor

zones/areas with a qualifying peak-shaving adjustment.7 However, as discussed below, this

provision requires clarification to ensure it functions as intended alongside PJM’s separate

Interim Resource Adequacy Service (“IRAS”) filing.

         PJM has made genuine progress toward a workable backstop mechanism, and it is against

that backdrop that United respectfully identifies, in the comments below, the specific

clarifications and commitments needed to ensure RBP achieves its intended purpose without

creating new barriers to the very resources best positioned to help.

         B. Some Elements of RBP Require Clarification or Further Commitment

         PJM indicated that it would accept discrete revisions from the Commission “where such

modification and/or severance is consistent with PJM’s overarching objectives in this filing.”8 In

this context, United respectfully offers the following opportunities to enhance the RBP, provided

that they can be implemented such that they do not “give[…] rise to complications” or cause

delay of the RBP and/or BRA for the 2029/2030 delivery year.9 The discrete recommendations

below aim to increase supply in the RBP and improve PJM’s overall resource adequacy outlook.

To the extent any of these recommendations would delay implementation of RBP, United

recognizes the urgency of the procurement and accepts the current design, though imperfect, as

good enough. United strongly urges, however, that PJM and the Commission commit to further




7
  Id at 44-45.
8
  Id at 3.
9
  Id.
                                                                                                  5
 reforms across all the areas identified below to improve outcomes beyond the RBP, and to ensure

that the RBP remains a one-time emergency measure.

               i.    Peak Shaving Adjustment Opt-Outs Should be Clarified

        As noted above, United supports PJM’s proposal to allow Electric Distributor zones/areas

with a qualifying peak shaving adjustment to opt out of a portion of their RBP obligation.10 This

opt-out recognizes that load which has already taken concrete steps to reduce its own

contribution to peak demand should not be treated the same as load that has done nothing to

address the shortfall it is helping to cause, and it gives Electric Distributors a meaningful

incentive to pursue peak shaving arrangements going forward.

        That incentive, however, depends entirely on the opt-out actually relieving the load in

question of backstop-related obligations, and PJM’s filing leaves that question unresolved. In its

RBP filing, PJM states that “even if the Electric Distributor zone/area qualifies for and receives

an opt-out from the RBP, the load in that zone/area may be subject to load reduction under the

forthcoming proposal to implement a IRAS.”11 PJM's now-filed IRAS proposal confirms this

concern rather than resolving it. Under the proposed Eligible New Large Load Amount formula,

a Large Load's exposure to IRAS curtailment is reduced only by its BYONC arrangements and

Allocated RBP UCAP MW; Peak Shaving Adjustment values, though separately tracked in the

Large Load Registry, play no role in that calculation.12 Read in the most concerning light, this

means a load that successfully qualifies for the RBP opt-out could nonetheless find itself subject

to IRAS curtailment on the same basis as load that made no effort to reduce its footprint at all, a



10
   Id at 44-45.
11
   Id, at 46.
12
   Proposed RAA, Attachment DD-4, § V(b) (PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Docket No. ER26-3515-000, Aug. 13,
2026); id. at 37 (Large Load Registry data field for Peak Shaving Adjustment value, tracked but not used in the
eligibility calculation).
                                                                                                                  6
 result that would undermine the very incentive the opt-out is meant to create. Clear,

unambiguous rules on this point are essential, both to actually entice Electric Distributors and

large loads to pursue peak shaving adjustments in the first place, and to give those that do the

confidence they will not face unexpected penalties or curtailment exposure down the line once

IRAS is filed. If Electric Distributors and their large-load customers cannot be confident that a

peak shaving adjustment actually reduces their exposure, whether through avoided RBP charges

or reduced curtailment priority under IRAS, many will have little reason to pursue the

arrangement in the first place.

       United recommends that the Commission direct PJM to amend the Eligible New Large

Load Amount formula in the IRAS proceeding, Docket No. ER26-3515-000, to credit Peak

Shaving Adjustment values on the same basis as BYONC and Allocated RBP UCAP MW, or to

explain on the record why a load managing its footprint through a state-sponsored peak shaving

program should be treated identically to one that has not. Absent such a change, the RBP opt-out

risks functioning as a paper protection rather than a substantive one, since PJM’s own IRAS

mechanics now confirm that a load's peak shaving efforts provide no relief from curtailment

exposure. While Tariff changes are not needed in the instant filing, United respectfully requests

that PJM clarify that Peak Shaving Adjustment will be taken into account when calculating IRAS

exposure, even if the zone/area still has some remaining curtailment risk.

       C. Unpredictable ELCC Values Carry Excessive Risk for Developers

       ELCC values for solar, storage, and other accredited resources are set by PJM based on

system-wide fleet mix and grid conditions that no individual developer can control, predict, or

hedge over a fifteen-year commitment. PJM’s proposal only partially addresses the risk this

uncertainty produces in the context of the RBP. Specifically, PJM allows developers to bid into

                                                                                                    7
 the RBP based on their own expectations of a resource’s future Effective Load Carrying

Capability (“ELCC”), including the ability to offer above the forecasted class rating, up to a

defined cap, where a developer believes its resource’s accreditation value is likely to improve

over the term.13 PJM also avoids applying shortfall charges to resources whose ELCC declines

below their committed RBP UCAP once they achieve commercial operation.14 This treatment is

a reasonable accommodation as far as it goes, but it does not go far enough: RBP resources

remain subject to unhedgeable ELCC risk in the revenue settlement for supply.

         Because that risk is effectively unhedgeable at the individual resource level, rational

developers will either choose not to participate in RBP or price a substantial risk premium into

their RBP offers to protect against it. This premium will exceed the actual expected cost of

ELCC variability and raise the cost of the RBP regardless of whether the risk materializes. A

better approach, consistent with proposals other stakeholders have put forward, would separate

this risk into its two component parts rather than assigning both to the developer.15 The portion

of ELCC decline that PJM can already forecast, based on known and projected fleet buildout,

should be published as an official long-term forecast covering the full RBP term, so that

developers can price that expected trajectory into their bids at face value, without needing to

guess at it or pad for it. The portion that cannot be forecast, meaning the variance above or below

that expected trajectory driven by factors outside any single developer’s control, should instead




13
   Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, § 18.5(e)(i) (Transmittal Letter at 55) (requiring RBP Sell Offers to state UCAP
MW based on the resource’s current ELCC Class Rating or unit-specific estimate, with sellers permitted to offer up
to 120% of that rating to reflect projected future improvement, at the seller’s own risk if the projection proves too
optimistic).
14
   Transmittal Letter at 87.
15
   See PJM Stakeholder Proposal of REV Renewables, LS Power, Middle River Power, and Geronimo Power, PJM
Reliability Backstop Procurement Design (submitted June 30, 2026) (“Proposing Companies' Alternative Proposal
vs. PJM Proposal”) https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-rbp/2026/20260630/20260630-
item-02k---rev-renewables--ls-power---mrp---geronimo---rbp---executive-summary.pdf
                                                                                                                   8
 be absorbed by RPM, where ELCC variability already manifests annually for every resource in

the fleet as a matter of course. Shifting that unhedgeable component to RPM, so long as an RBP

resource’s underlying installed capacity remains unchanged, would allow ratepayers to bear the

actual cost of ELCC variability as it occurs, rather than an inflated risk premium embedded in

every RBP bid whether or not that variability ever materializes. The practical result should be

lower, more competitive RBP offers at equivalent or lower total cost to load.

        Addressing this risk is not simply a matter of fairness to developers, it bears directly on

whether the RBP achieves its stated reliability purpose. An inflated risk premium does not just

raise the price load pays for capacity that clears, it risks excluding resources from clearing at all.

Because PJM’s proposed maximum willingness to pay is fixed as a MW-weighted average

levelized cost across all selected offers, resources forced to bid in an unhedgeable ELCC risk

premium are more likely to price above that cap, or above where competing offers clear, and be

passed over in the selection process entirely. Every resource priced out of the RBP on that basis

is capacity that does not get procured toward the Final RBP Target, increasing the chance that

the target is not reached. These resources also bring reliability value beyond their raw UCAP

contribution. For example, storage paired with solar helps shift midday generation into the

evening hours when PJM’s system is most at risk, and a resource mix that includes solar and

storage alongside gas reduces PJM’s exposure to the kind of correlated, fuel-supply-driven

failures that have caused widespread forced outages among gas generation during past extreme

cold weather events.16 Excluding or discouraging these resources through avoidable pricing risk




16
   See “Winter Storm Elliott: Event Analysis and Recommendation Report” PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. at Page 49
(July 17,2023) (Of the total 49,959 MW forced outages 33,404 or 71% was natural gas facilities.)
https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/library/reports-notices/special-reports/2023/20230717-winter-storm-elliott-
event-analysis-and-recommendation-report.pdf.
                                                                                                             9
 not only harms individual developers, it narrows the diversity and resilience of the resource mix

the RBP is meant to secure.

       United further notes that ELCC uncertainty is compounded for DER Aggregation

Resources by factors distinct from those affecting utility-scale solar and storage. The

accreditation methodology PJM applies to behind-the-meter aggregated resources depends not

only on fleet-wide modeling assumptions, but also on PJM’s still-evolving rules for how

distributed resources are modeled, dispatched, and measured, including ongoing changes to

metering, telemetry, and baseline methodologies that can independently shift a DER

aggregation’s accredited value from one delivery year to the next. Any commitment PJM makes

to enhance ELCC forecasting and accreditation stability should expressly cover DER

Aggregation Resources, not solely utility-scale resource classes, so that aggregators bidding into

the RBP or future capacity procurements can price their offers based on a published, transparent

forecast rather than guessing at both fleet-wide ELCC dynamics and PJM’s own methodological

evolution simultaneously.

       United requests, at a minimum, that PJM commit to enhancing its ELCC forecasting and

accreditation process in the near term to promote greater stability and predictability for all

capacity resources, whether bidding into RBP, the RPM, and/or pursuing other long-term

commitments. Doing so would benefit not only the RBP procurement itself, but investment

confidence in PJM’s capacity market more broadly, which is ultimately essential to supporting

durable resource adequacy outcomes across the region. Absent such action, PJM risks




                                                                                                 10
 perpetuating an uncertain investment environment that has contributed to the region’s failure to

bring on new resources to address its growing reliability shortfall.

        D. Exclusion of Surplus Interconnection Service from RBP is a missed opportunity

        PJM recognized SIS as a tool to address “the need for more Capacity on the PJM

Transmission System from resources that can be brought online quickly” when it proposed

reforms to its SIS process in 2024, approved by FERC in 2025, to “encourage and facilitate the

use of Surplus Interconnection Service from existing and planned generating units on PJM’s

system.”17 Despite significant progress, barriers to full utilization of SIS remain, and this filing

misses an opportunity to capitalize on SIS as a pathway to accelerate capacity additions.

        PJM’s proposal draws a sharp line between the criteria for capacity that may offset a

load’s RBP obligation and the criteria for capacity eligible to be sold into the RBP as an RBP

Resource, and Surplus Interconnection Service capacity falls on the favorable side of that line for

one purpose and the unfavorable side for the other: new load may use SIS-derived capacity to

reduce its own RBP obligation,18 but a resource relying on SIS is expressly barred from selling

into the RBP as an RBP Resource.19 PJM’s stated rationale for the exclusion turns principally on

the difficulty of cleanly attributing UCAP between an existing host resource and a surplus

addition, which PJM states “creat[es] uncertainty and the need for sensitivities or estimates” in

both the incremental capacity determination and RBP settlement.20 PJM’s reasoning treats SIS-

based capacity as real and valuable enough to net against a load’s RBP obligation, yet not

reliable enough to sell into the RBP, even though the underlying physical capacity is identical


17
    PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. “Proposed Tariff Amendments for Surplus Interconnection Service” Docket No.
ER25-778-000 (filed Dec 20, 2024), Transmittal Letter at 6.
18
    Transmittal Letter at 36. (Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, § 18.2(a)(iii))
19
   Id at 53 (“[R]esources relying on Surplus Interconnection Service to bring new UCAP MW on the PJM system do
not qualify as RBP Resources, because these resources do not have any independent rights to the PJM system.”).
20
    Croop Affidavit at P 20 (Transmittal Letter at 53-54).
                                                                                                            11
 either way.21 United is concerned by PJM’s decision to leave valuable SIS capacity on the

sidelines, and urges the Commission and PJM to act quickly to increase SIS opportunities, for

two reasons.

         First, SIS is a uniquely fast-to-deploy resource, and allowing SIS-based capacity to

contribute to addressing PJM’s resource adequacy challenges should be a priority independent of

the RBP. SIS was designed specifically to bring new capacity online faster than a full

interconnection study process would otherwise allow, by making use of interconnection rights an

existing resource is not fully utilizing.22 At a moment when PJM has determined that a 6,831.3

MW UCAP shortfall requires an unprecedented 15-year backstop procurement mechanism,23

PJM should simultaneously be doing everything it can to ensure that one of the fastest-to-market

sources of new capacity is actually facilitating new capacity additions in practice.

         Second, and relatedly, this is not the only barrier limiting the full use of SIS to deliver

new capacity to PJM. Current market participation rules do not provide a meaningful pathway in

practice for SIS based resources to bring new capacity onto the system. A surplus resource that

wishes to participate in PJM’s markets must either hybridize with the original interconnection

customer, which generally requires unwinding existing commercial obligations; or abandon its

SIS-based interconnection status and instead pursue a full interconnection study to obtain its own

incremental Capacity Interconnection Rights and Maximum Facility Output, co-located with the

existing host resource.24 PJM's own affidavit confirms that this is true for the RBP specifically as

(Transmittal Letter at 53–54).
22
   Croop Affidavit at P 17.
23
   Id at P 4.
24
   Id at P18 (“[T]hese sited projects would still have an opportunity to offer into the RBP and co-locate with the
existing resource and be studied by PJM for increased CIRs and MFO at the facility through the interconnection
process.”).
                                                                                                                     12
 well: a surplus resource's only path to participate in the RBP is this same full interconnection

process, not its existing SIS arrangement.25 In other words, current market participation rules

effectively restrict meaningful capacity participation, in the RBP or otherwise, by SIS resources,

undermining the speed-to-market advantage that makes these resources valuable in the first

place. To take the common example of storage added to an existing solar site, SIS only grants

capacity interconnection rights (“CIRs”) if the storage merges into the solar plant as a single

hybrid resource. However, this pathway typically requires unwinding existing PPA, tax equity,

and lender agreements, which is rarely feasible on an operating asset. If storage instead

interconnects independently as a co-located resource, it must participate in PJM markets as

energy-only—forfeiting all capacity accreditation and preventing SIS from serving as a tool to

expedite accredited capacity entry in PJM. United recommends that PJM address this barrier

both within the RBP and more broadly across its capacity market participation rules.

            Within the RBP, United recommends that the Commission direct PJM to allow the

incremental UCAP created by an SIS-based addition, meaning the difference between the

resulting hybrid resource's UCAP and what the host resource's UCAP would have been on a

standalone basis, to qualify for the RBP. This approach directly resolves PJM’s stated concern

regarding unclear UCAP attribution between the existing resource and the surplus addition,26

because it does not require PJM to determine how much of the hybrid resource’s total UCAP

belongs to which component. It instead isolates and credits only the new value created by the

surplus addition, a discrete and calculable quantity, while leaving the host resource’s pre-

     Id.
26
     Id at P 20.
                                                                                                   13
 existing UCAP contribution untouched and outside the RBP altogether. This should be a discrete

and surgical adjustment to RBP eligibility.

         Separate and apart from RBP, United requests that PJM commit to expand opportunities

for SIS-based resources in PJM's capacity market, so that this same fast-to-deploy source of

capacity is not permanently forced to choose between hybridization or a full interconnection

study as its only options to deliver new capacity to PJM. Specifically, United requests that PJM

commit to a broader stakeholder review that would consider the following solutions:

     •   Settle UCAP into two accounts. Keep CIRs pooled under a single GIA—no allocation

         or division required—but settle the resulting UCAP between two capacity market

         participant accounts, one for solar and one for the battery. Because a hybrid resource

         behind one set of CIRs generates more combined UCAP than the same two assets would

         under any divided-CIR approach, this option preserves the most total UCAP while still

         giving each owner an independently recognized, bankable capacity position. One

         reasonable way to handle UCAP allocations would be to allocate the existing resource

         whatever it would have gotten without the hybrid addition and then to allocate the

         remaining UCAP to the addition. Capacity market revenues, PAI obligations, and PAI

         liability would flow to each account according to this split.

     •   Independent E&AS participation. Allow the component parts of a hybrid resource to

         participate independently in Energy & Ancillary Services markets. PJM has already

         indicated interest in exploring this pathway in its “Hybrid Resources Market Model

         Selection” Problem Statement / Issue Charge.27 Capacity market revenue still has to be

market-model-selection---issue-charge.pdf.
                                                                                                          14
          disaggregated ex post between the two owners in many cases, but this model has attracted

         significant developer interest.

     •   CIR transfer between components. Enable CIR transfers between the components of a

         co-located resource, so each party can hold, finance, and transfer its own share.

         Suppliers—not a fixed ELCC proportional formula—should determine how CIRs are

         allocated between them. This would resemble the CIR transfer process that is available to

         deactivating generators, i.e., this would enable CIR transfers for resources that are

         partially giving up capacity resource status. It would be appropriate to require that any

         transfer only be allowed if it resulted in a net increase in system UCAP.

Pursuing these reforms to SIS will not deliver more capacity through the RBP, but it will make

additional capacity available in upcoming BRAs and via bring your own new capacity

arrangements, and thus help to resolve tight resource adequacy conditions that are expected to

persist beyond the RBP. The Commission can encourage progress from PJM to fully realize its

goal to “encourage and facilitate the use of Surplus Interconnection Service” as a tool to bring

more capacity onto its system quickly28; and, if progress is not made, take further action to

ensure a fully functional SIS process in PJM.

         E. Restrictions to DR/DER Participation will Limit RBP Participation of
            Affordable, Fast-to-Deploy Resources

         Demand-side resources and demand response are among the most affordable and flexible

solutions to address PJM’s resource adequacy shortfall, capable of being deployed on timescales

of three to twenty-four months, alongside generation resources that may target later commercial




28
   “Proposed Tariff Amendments for Surplus Interconnection Service” Docket No. ER25-778-000 Transmittal Letter
at 6. (December 20, 2024)
                                                                                                           15
 operation dates.29 PJM has offered some promising opportunities to deploy more of these

resources in the instant filing, but has simultaneously erected unnecessary barriers. As with

Surplus Interconnection Service, PJM applies materially different eligibility standards to

Demand Response and DER Aggregation Resources depending on whether they are offsetting a

load’s own RBP obligation or competing to sell into the RBP as RBP Resources. While both

pathways suffer deficiencies, they can be remedied through surgical changes that will expand DR

and DER availability and help to close PJM’s resource adequacy gap.

                                        a. Qualifying RBP Offset MW Rules for DR and DERs
                                           Should be Clarified

        To offset an RBP obligation, DR/DER can provide Qualifying RBP Offset MW either as

a new supply resource or through direct enrollment of a new load as an Annual Demand

Response or DER Capacity Aggregation Resource. United supports these pathways. However,

the latter is described as a bridge mechanism pending the availability of generation or storage

capacity not yet in service.30 United does not oppose the option for DR/DER to serve as a bridge

mechanism, but also urges against artificially constraining Demand Response and DER

Aggregation Resources to serve as temporary solutions. Demand-side resources and demand

response deliver standing capacity, energy, and transmission congestion relief benefits that

persist independent of whether new generation or storage capacity comes online; they are not

merely a placeholder for supply that has not yet materialized. PJM’s Tariff and this proceeding

should recognize Demand Response and DER Aggregation Resources as a durable, permanent




29
   Voltus, Inc., Submission to the PJM Board, Critical Issue Fast Path Stage 4, Reliability Backstop Procurement /
Connect & Manage, at 1 (June 2026). https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/cifp-
rbp/2026/20260630/20260630-item-02l---voltus---cm-and-rbp---executive-summary.pdf
30
   Transmittal Letter at 40.
                                                                                                                 16
 component of the resource mix addressing PJM’s shortfall, not solely as an interim measure to be

phased out or superseded once other capacity arrives.

           A related ambiguity in the offset pathway itself warrants clarification. Proposed Tariff,

Attachment DD, § 18.2(c) offers Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW status through three

evidentiary pathways, but it is unclear whether behind-the-meter generation or storage backing a

demand response arrangement may rely on the signed bilateral contract pathway in § 18.2(c)(i),

available on equal terms to front-of-the-meter resources, or whether it is instead confined to the

demand response pathway in § 18.2(c)(iii), which imposes two requirements not applicable

under (c)(i): that the resource offset the new load's full MW quantity rather than a partial share,

and that it be in place by the 2028/2029 Delivery Year Second Incremental Auction or the load

purchase replacement offset capacity. United requests that PJM clarify that behind-the-meter

generation and storage backing a demand response arrangement is not categorically confined to

III.    PJM MUST BE HELD ACCOUNTABLE FOR ENSURING THAT RBP

        REMAINS A ONE-TIME MECHANISM

             A. RBP is Specifically Designed as a One-Time Mechanism

        PJM’s own filing provides the clearest evidence that RBP is meant to be a bounded, non-

recurring response to the shortfall identified in the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction, and PJM

should be held to that characterization going forward. United understands that PJM has

represented RBP as a one-time mechanism and takes PJM at its word on that point. United

nonetheless requests assurance that steps will be taken to ensure this characterization holds in

practice, so that RBP does not become a recurring tool PJM invokes each time a future auction

reveals a shortfall.

        Most notably, PJM defends its choice of a pay-as-bid clearing structure, rather than the

uniform clearing price design PJM otherwise favors across its markets,45 specifically on the

ground that the RBP “is not designed to be a durable or repeatable procurement,” such that “its

pricing outcomes are less likely to serve as incentive market signals.”46 PJM further explains that

because RBP resources will differ in contract duration, commercial operation date, and ELCC

accreditation over the term, they do not constitute a single homogeneous product suited to

uniform pricing, a rationale that only holds together if RBP is understood as a one-time, purpose-

Having justified a significant departure from its preferred market design specifically because

RBP is one-time and non-repeatable, PJM should not be permitted to invoke RBP, or a

substantially similar mechanism, as a recurring tool each time a future Base Residual Auction

reveals a shortfall.

        United recommends that the Commission condition its approval of this filing on an

explicit acknowledgment that RBP is a one-time mechanism addressed specifically to resolve the

shortfall identified in the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction, and not a template PJM may invoke

unilaterally in response to future shortfalls without a fresh stakeholder process and a new Section

205 filing subject to the Commission’s full review. Such a condition would simply hold PJM to

the premise on which it has already built its own pay-as-bid justification, and would ensure that

any future backstop procurement, should one prove necessary, is developed with the benefit of a

new stakeholder process reflecting conditions and lessons learned at that time, rather than treated

as a foregone conclusion based on this proceeding.

            B. RBP Must be Followed by a Commitment to Durable Reforms

The 6,831.3 MW shortfall identified in the 2028/2029 Base Residual Auction is itself the product

for purpose, and requires holistic reform.48 New entry has been further hampered by persistent

interconnection queue delays, evolving supply chain constraints, and permitting timelines,

barriers documented in United’s own analysis, which found that PJM had the largest

IV.      RETAIL COST ALLOCATION - SUPPORTING STATE/LARGE LOAD
         COORDINATION

         The fairness premise underlying PJM’s proposed cost allocation framework, that large

loads should bear the cost of the capacity procured on their account, depends on state and

Relevant Electric Retail Regulatory Authority (“RERRA”) action that PJM’s proposal cannot

itself guarantee.52 PJM’s allocation stops at the LSE level, using a state or RERRA-determined

RBP Obligation where one is reported, or a default Peak Load Contribution ratio share where it

is not.53 Whether the cost that lands on an LSE is then actually passed through to the large load

causing it, or spread across an LSE’s broader retail base, is a retail ratemaking question entirely

outside PJM’s proposal and, as PJM itself acknowledges, outside the Commission’s

jurisdiction.54

Corporation Commission and the Data Center Coalition, in which the parties committed to

jointly develop model state retail tariff provisions addressing RBP retail cost allocation by
